## Effect on electronics

Cosmic rays have sufficient energy to alter the states of circuit components in electronic integrated circuits, causing transient errors to occur (such as corrupted data in electronic memory devices or incorrect performance of CPUs) often referred to as "soft errors". This has been a problem in electronics at extremely high-altitude, such as in satellites, but with transistors becoming smaller and smaller, this is becoming an increasing concern in ground-level electronics as well. Studies by IBM in the 1990s suggest that computers typically experience about one cosmic-ray-induced error per 256 megabytes of RAM per month. To alleviate this problem, the Intel Corporation has proposed a cosmic ray detector that could be integrated into future high-density microprocessors, allowing the processor to repeat the last command following a cosmic-ray event. ECC memory is used to protect data against data corruption caused by cosmic rays.

In 2008, data corruption in a flight control system caused an Airbus A330 airliner to twice plunge hundreds of feet, resulting in injuries to multiple passengers and crew members. Cosmic rays were investigated among other possible causes of the data corruption, but were ultimately ruled out as being very unlikely.

In August 2020, scientists reported that ionizing radiation from environmental radioactive materials and cosmic rays may substantially limit the coherence times of qubits if they are not shielded adequately which may be critical for realizing fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers in the future.
## Significance to aerospace travel

Galactic cosmic rays are one of the most important barriers standing in the way of plans for interplanetary travel by crewed spacecraft. Cosmic rays also pose a threat to electronics placed aboard outgoing probes. In 2010, a malfunction aboard the Voyager 2 space probe was credited to a single flipped bit, probably caused by a cosmic ray. Strategies such as physical or magnetic shielding for spacecraft have been considered in order to minimize the damage to electronics and human beings caused by cosmic rays.

On 31 May 2013, NASA scientists reported that a possible crewed mission to Mars may involve a greater radiation risk than previously believed, based on the amount of energetic particle radiation detected by the RAD on the Mars Science Laboratory while traveling from the Earth to Mars in 2011–2012.

Flying 12 kilometres (39,000 ft) high, passengers and crews of jet airliners are exposed to at least 10 times the cosmic ray dose that people at sea level receive. Aircraft flying polar routes near the geomagnetic poles are at particular risk.
## Role in lightning

Cosmic rays have been implicated in the triggering of electrical breakdown in lightning. It has been proposed that essentially all lightning is triggered through a relativistic process, or "runaway breakdown", seeded by cosmic ray secondaries. Subsequent development of the lightning discharge then occurs through "conventional breakdown" mechanisms.
## Postulated role in climate change

A role for cosmic rays in climate was suggested by Edward P. Ney in 1959 and by Robert E. Dickinson in 1975. It has been postulated that cosmic rays may have been responsible for major climatic change and mass extinction in the past. According to Adrian Mellott and Mikhail Medvedev, 62-million-year cycles in biological marine populations correlate with the motion of the Earth relative to the galactic plane and increases in exposure to cosmic rays. The researchers suggest that this and gamma ray bombardments deriving from local supernovae could have affected cancer and mutation rates, and might be linked to decisive alterations in the Earth's climate, and to the mass extinctions of the Ordovician.

Danish physicist Henrik Svensmark has controversially argued that because solar variation modulates the cosmic ray flux on Earth, it would consequently affect the rate of cloud formation and hence be an indirect cause of global warming. Svensmark is one of several scientists outspokenly opposed to the mainstream scientific assessment of global warming, leading to concerns that the proposition that cosmic rays are connected to global warming could be ideologically biased rather than scientifically based. Other scientists have vigorously criticized Svensmark for sloppy and inconsistent work: one example is adjustment of cloud data that understates error in lower cloud data, but not in high cloud data; another example is "incorrect handling of the physical data" resulting in graphs that do not show the correlations they claim to show. Despite Svensmark's assertions, galactic cosmic rays have shown no statistically significant influence on changes in cloud cover, and have been demonstrated in studies to have no causal relationship to changes in global temperature.
## Possible mass extinction factor

A handful of studies have identified chronological overlap between nearby supernova activity and the end‑Pliocene marine megafaunal extinction epoch. Some researchers have hypothesised that the associated increase in radiation exposure could have acted as an extinction driver for marine life, although the idea remains tentative and contested.
## Potential role in biological evolution

Cosmic rays, as a form of ionizing radiation, can, in principle, interact with biomolecules. A minority of researchers have speculated that long‑term or episodic variations in cosmic‑ray flux—for example following nearby supernovae or changes in heliospheric or geomagnetic shielding—could have influenced evolutionary processes on Earth.

High‑energy primary particles and their secondary cascades can produce ionisation and chemical damage that increases background mutation rates in exposed organisms. Cosmic‑ray–driven changes in atmospheric chemistry (for example, ozone depletion with consequent increases in surface ultraviolet flux) could alter selection pressures and ecological conditions. A small body of theoretical work has also proposed that magnetically influenced or spin-polarized radiation might bias the formation or destruction rates of chiral molecules; this idea is usually discussed in origin‑of‑life or homochirality contexts rather than as a primary driver of later macroevolution.

Direct empirical evidence linking variations in cosmic‑ray flux to macroevolutionary patterns is limited. Laboratory and modelling studies show that ionizing radiation can cause molecular damage and mutations, and astrophysical and geochemical work documents episodes of enhanced cosmic radiation, but robust, multidisciplinary demonstrations (for example temporally correlated geochemical markers and biological signals with clear causal chains) are lacking. Most recent reviews treat cosmic‑ray‑driven evolution as a plausible but unproven set of hypotheses.

o-ov-seeing: For almost all of human history, astronomy meant visible light: the narrow band of colours our eyes can see. But visible light is a tiny sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum, which stretches from radio waves, with wavelengths from millimetres to kilometres, through infrared, visible and ultraviolet, to X-rays and gamma rays. Each band reveals a different universe. And in the last few decades we have learned to listen to the cosmos with messengers that are not light at all: neutrinos and gravitational waves. This section is about those other ways of seeing, and above all about radio astronomy, which has done more than any other to reveal the early universe.

Radio astronomy began by accident. In 1932, Karl Jansky, an engineer at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New Jersey, was hunting for sources of static that might interfere with transatlantic radio telephone calls. He found a faint hiss that rose and set with the stars, and traced it to the centre of our galaxy. An American amateur, Grote Reber, built a dish in his back garden in Illinois in 1937 and made the first radio map of the sky. After the Second World War, radar engineers turned their skills to the heavens. In Britain, Bernard Lovell set up at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire, where the great steerable dish now called the Lovell Telescope was completed in 1957, just in time to track the rocket that carried Sputnik into orbit. At Cambridge, Martin Ryle developed the technique of combining several antennas to act as one giant telescope, which earned him a Nobel prize.

Radio telescopes work differently from optical ones. A dish collects radio waves and focuses them onto a receiver, which measures their strength and timing very precisely. Because radio waves are long, a single dish sees the sky blurrily, unless it is enormous. The answer is interferometry: linking many dishes and combining their signals, so that the array behaves like a single telescope as wide as the greatest distance between its dishes. The Very Large Array in New Mexico, ALMA high in the Chilean Andes, and the Square Kilometre Array now under construction in South Africa and Australia all work this way. Push the idea to its limit and you get the Event Horizon Telescope, which links dishes across the whole Earth to make a virtual telescope the size of the planet. In 2019 it produced the first image of the shadow of a black hole, in the galaxy Messier 87, and in 2022 the image of Sagittarius A star, the black hole at the heart of our own galaxy.

What does radio reveal that optical telescopes cannot? It sees through dust, which hides the centre of our galaxy and the nurseries where stars are born. It sees cold gas: atomic hydrogen, the most common element, broadcasts a faint signal at a wavelength of twenty-one centimetres, and molecules in cold clouds have their own radio fingerprints. It discovered pulsars, spinning neutron stars found by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967, and quasars, the blazing hearts of distant galaxies powered by giant black holes. And it found the cosmic microwave background itself, the afterglow of the Big Bang. Today, radio astronomers are hunting for the faint twenty-one centimetre signal of hydrogen from the cosmic Dark Ages and dawn, stretched by the expansion to long radio wavelengths. A claimed detection by the EDGES experiment in 2018 caused great excitement, but has not been confirmed, and arrays such as HERA, LOFAR and the coming low frequency part of the Square Kilometre Array aim to map the signal properly.

Beyond radio, there are other windows. X-ray telescopes in space, such as Chandra and XMM-Newton, see gas at millions of degrees in clusters of galaxies and matter falling into black holes. Infrared telescopes, above all the James Webb Space Telescope, see the stretched light of the first galaxies and peer into dusty clouds. Gamma-ray telescopes catch the most violent explosions. Neutrino observatories, such as Super-Kamiokande in Japan and IceCube buried in the Antarctic ice, catch ghostly particles from the Sun, exploding stars and distant galaxies. And since 2015, the LIGO and Virgo detectors have heard gravitational waves from colliding black holes and neutron stars, opening an entirely new sense. When these messengers are combined, as in 2017 when merging neutron stars were seen in gravitational waves and every kind of light at once, astronomers call it multi-messenger astronomy. This section tells the stories of the instruments, the people who built them, and what they have found.
o-r01: If our eyes could see radio waves, the night sky would look completely different. The bright stars we know would almost vanish, because stars are faint radio sources. Instead, the band of the Milky Way would glow brilliantly, brightest of all towards the galactic centre in Sagittarius. Here and there would be intense points of light: the remains of exploded stars, such as Cassiopeia A, the brightest radio source in the sky beyond the Sun; vast double lobes of radio emission stretching from distant galaxies, powered by jets from giant black holes; and the Sun itself, flaring and crackling. And behind everything, filling the whole sky evenly, would be a faint glow at millimetre wavelengths: the cosmic microwave background.

Radio waves are produced by different processes from visible light. Hot objects, such as stars, glow mostly in visible light. Radio waves come mainly from three kinds of source. First, from electrons spiralling at nearly the speed of light in magnetic fields, which produce what is called synchrotron radiation; this traces the most violent places in the universe, such as supernova remnants, pulsars and the jets of active galaxies. Second, from very cold things: the microwave background at under three degrees above absolute zero, and cold dust and gas in the clouds where stars form. Third, from atoms and molecules emitting at specific wavelengths, like a radio station broadcasting on its own frequency.

The most important of these is the twenty-one centimetre line of hydrogen. Neutral hydrogen gas, the raw material of stars and galaxies, emits this faint signal when the electron in a hydrogen atom flips its spin. Because hydrogen is everywhere, the line lets radio astronomers map the gas throughout our galaxy, revealing its spiral arms, which are hidden from optical telescopes by dust. In the 1950s, Dutch and Australian radio astronomers used it to make the first map of the Milky Way's spiral structure. It also lets them measure how fast gas is orbiting in other galaxies, far beyond the visible stars, which provided some of the strongest evidence for dark matter. And because the expansion of the universe stretches the line to longer wavelengths, radio telescopes tuned to different frequencies can see hydrogen at different times in cosmic history, back to the Dark Ages.

Molecules are just as useful. Cold clouds of gas contain carbon monoxide, water, ammonia, alcohol and hundreds of other molecules, many discovered by their radio signatures. They reveal where new stars and planets are forming, and even the chemistry of planet-forming discs around young stars, which ALMA has imaged with stunning clarity, showing rings and gaps carved, perhaps, by young planets.

Radio sees through dust. The centre of our galaxy is hidden behind so much dust that only one part in a trillion of its visible light reaches us. But radio waves pass straight through. That is how astronomers found Sagittarius A star, the compact radio source at the galactic centre, in 1974, and how the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of its black hole in 2022.

Radio has made extraordinary discoveries by accident. Quasars were first found as radio sources in the late 1950s and early 1960s; when Maarten Schmidt measured the redshift of one, three C two seven three, in 1963, he realised it was billions of light years away and therefore enormously powerful. In 1967, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a research student at Cambridge, noticed a bit of scruff on her chart recorder that turned out to be regular pulses every one and a third seconds: the first pulsar, a spinning neutron star. Pulsars are now used as cosmic clocks, so precise that networks of them, called pulsar timing arrays, have detected the faint background of gravitational waves washing through our galaxy. And in 2007, astronomers found fast radio bursts, millisecond flashes from distant galaxies, whose signals are smeared by the gas they pass through, allowing the thin gas between galaxies to be weighed.

Above all, radio gave cosmology its most important piece of evidence: the cosmic microwave background, found by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson with a horn antenna in New Jersey in 1965. Without radio astronomy, we would know far less about the early universe. And with the Square Kilometre Array, and perhaps one day radio telescopes on the far side of the Moon, radio may give us our first direct view of the cosmic Dark Ages.
